title: A chemist measured the age of the Earth.
description:
A chemist measured the age of the Earth. Clair Patterson used lead from the Canyon Diablo meteorite and got 4.55 billion years, give or take 70 million.

His samples kept coming out contaminated. He found lead throughout his laboratory, even in his own hair.

He built one of the first clean rooms. He acid-cleaned his apparatus and distilled every chemical shipped to him.

The lead in the air was not natural. Ice cores from Greenland in 1964 and Antarctica in 1965 showed atmospheric lead rising soon after tetraethyl lead was introduced.

Modern bones held far more lead than ancient ones. He reported a rise of 700 to 1200 fold against 1600 year old Peruvian skeletons.

The lead industry pushed back. He was excluded from a 1971 National Research Council panel on atmospheric lead.

Completely banned for road vehicles in the United States on 1 January 1996.

He set out to date the Earth and ended up cleaning its air.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clair_Cameron_Patterson: read in full (carries a maintenance banner and some citation needed tags; only untagged statements were used). Established the 1956 paper giving 4.550 Gy plus or minus 70 My from Canyon Diablo lead isotopes; the lead contamination found throughout his laboratory including in his own hair; one of the first laboratory clean rooms, acid-cleaned apparatus and distilled chemicals; Greenland ice cores (Camp Century, 1964) and Antarctic cores (1965) showing atmospheric lead rising after tetraethyl lead; the 700 to 1200 fold rise in lead in modern bones against 1600 year old Peruvian skeletons; exclusion from a 1971 National Research Council panel; and the complete US ban on leaded road petrol on 1 January 1996.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Earth: read (first 39,400 of 60,257 characters verbatim). Confirmed 4.55 plus or minus 0.07 billion years, determined by Patterson on several meteorites including Canyon Diablo and published in 1956.
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetraethyllead: read (first 39,400 of 83,992 characters verbatim). Confirmed the total elimination of leaded petrol sales for on-road vehicles on 1 January 1996, and the Ethyl Corporation lobbying against restrictions.
